column3: The Hebrew repeats the affordability phrase “what his hand reaches”; BSB omits that phrase here after expressing affordability in the preceding verse.
The Hebrew expresses inability with “his hand does not reach”; BSB says “cannot afford the cost.”
The Hebrew has both “spoke” and “saying”; BSB condenses these to “said.”
The Hebrew repeats the possession language in “a house in the land of your possession”; BSB says “a house in that land.”
The Hebrew says the mark has appeared “to me in the house”; BSB says “has appeared in my house.”
The Hebrew names “the priest” three times; BSB names him twice and uses “he” for the other occurrence.
The Hebrew says to examine “the affliction” and introduces the finding with “behold”; BSB says to examine “the house” and introduces it with “if.”
The Hebrew repeats “the house” three times; BSB names it once and uses “it” for closing it up.
The Hebrew introduces the spread with “behold”; BSB uses “If” and supplies “the house” as the object of inspection.
The Hebrew uses active plural verbs for removing and throwing out the stones; BSB uses passive verbs.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew changes from plural “they shall take” and “bring” to singular “he shall take” and “plaster”; BSB uses a passive construction without that change in number.
The Hebrew says the affliction returns “and blossoms”; BSB combines the two actions as “reappears.”
The Hebrew introduces the spread with “behold”; BSB introduces it with “If.”
The Hebrew has active singular verbs for tearing down and taking out the house materials; BSB uses passive “be torn down” and “taken.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew gives sleeping and eating separate clauses, repeating the clothes-washing command; BSB joins them with “or” under a single washing command.
The Hebrew emphasizes coming with a repeated verb and says the affliction “has healed”; BSB gives the coming verb once and says the mildew “is gone.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls the water “living water”; BSB says “fresh water.”
The Hebrew calls the water “living water”; BSB says “fresh water.”
The Hebrew calls the water “living water”; BSB says “fresh water.”
The Hebrew names singular “the field”; BSB uses plural “the open fields.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew joins the clothing and house with “and”; BSB uses “or.”
The Hebrew joins all three conditions with “and”; BSB uses “or” before the last.
The Hebrew lists the unclean day before the clean day and ends with the single disease term; BSB reverses the clean/unclean order and expands the final term to “skin diseases and mildew.”
